Completeness is equivalently identified by comparing the ring with its maximal-ideal-adic completion.
The going-down condition uses inclusion chains of primes of the source spectrum.
The going-up condition uses inclusion chains of primes of the source spectrum.
A category-valued presheaf is defined by a contravariant functor into categories.
A split fibred category must first be a Grothendieck fibration over its base.
A splitting arises from a strict contravariant category-valued functor through Grothendieck construction.
A discrete valuation ring is a valuation ring with the specified discrete ordered value group.
Domination is defined for an inclusion of local rings by contraction of maximal ideals.
Perfectness is defined by requiring that all algebraic extensions be separable.
Limit ordinals are a special kind of ordinal characterized by not being successors.
The limit-ordinal criterion excludes the successor of any smaller ordinal.
A successor ordinal is constructed by adjoining the previous ordinal as an element.
The graded module construction presupposes a nonnegatively graded coefficient ring.
This summand condition is an equivalent characterization of projectivity, not a separate kind of projective module.
The dimension of a finite module is defined as the Krull dimension of its support.
The dimension of a module uses topological Krull dimension of the support subspace.
The finite-module support is the module support notion specialized to a finitely generated module.
The special support statement is explicitly restricted to finitely generated modules.
Local freeness is defined by asking module localizations to be free on a cover.
A contravariant functor from C is an ordinary functor defined on the opposite category.
The representable presheaf is a functor whose source is the opposite category.
A representable presheaf is a contravariant functor given by Hom into an object.
The Zariski topology on a scheme is specified by requiring affine charts to carry the prime-spectrum topology.
The Zariski topology is defined on the underlying space of a scheme.
Categories over a fixed base form a strict 2-category with projection-preserving functors and natural transformations.
Universal closedness of a continuous map is tested after arbitrary pullbacks, which are categorical fibre products.
The quasi-regular sequence criterion compares naturally graded modules over a polynomial coefficient ring.
The Hom-functor criterion for projectivity depends on exactness of the represented functor in the category of modules.
The Bourbaki-properness criterion is expressed through products of topological spaces and the induced product map.
The diagonal criterion uses the product topological space X×X, a categorical product in the category of spaces.
An abelian group is explicitly a group satisfying an additional commutativity axiom; abstract group is the prerequisite.
The additive structure of this associative ring is required to be an abelian group, independently of whether unity is assumed.
The definition of a two-sided ideal requires the parent ring's addition and both multiplication actions.
A commutative prime ideal must first be an ideal; the extra product test and properness distinguish primality.
A commutative unital ring satisfies the underlying associative ring axioms; the target is a broad structural prerequisite, not a claim that unity is optional here.
A general left module uses an abelian additive group as its underlying module addition structure.
The left scalar action is defined over an associative ring; a separate source-specific unit axiom may be added.
Regularity of a Noetherian ring is defined by regularity of each prime localization, which requires the local ring notion.
The exact source definition assumes a Noetherian commutative ring and then imposes regularity of all prime localizations.
Vector addition is required to form an abelian group; the scalar-action axioms further specialize this additive structure.
A group action uses the multiplication and identity element of the acting group; abstract group is the prerequisite.
A topological group carries a group structure before continuity of multiplication and inversion is imposed.
The topology making a group topological is a topology on its underlying set, requiring the topological-space notion.
The continuity conditions in a topological ring require the underlying algebraic ring structure first.
A topological ring is a ring endowed with a topology on its underlying set, with continuous algebraic operations.
The finite-generation condition presupposes an R-module. In this commutative setting the left-module structure is appropriate, with the unital convention made explicit.
The Noetherian ring condition quantifies over all its ideals, requiring the ideal notion before the finiteness property.
The Noetherian property is an additional finiteness condition on an underlying commutative ring, a special case of associative ring.
The prime spectrum has prime ideals of a commutative ring as its points; the proper prime-ideal definition supplies them.
A prime element is characterized through the primality of its principal ideal in an integral domain, hence the commutative prime-ideal meaning is prerequisite.
Localization starts with a commutative ring, which is an associative ring, and then constructs a fraction ring.
Normality in this formulation requires localizing at every prime ideal of a commutative ring.
The normal-ring property is imposed on an underlying commutative ring before local integrally closed domains are considered.
Geometric regularity requires regularity of each relevant scalar-extension ring. For a Noetherian algebra under finite extensions these are Noetherian regular rings.

The Stacks 10.32.1 nilpotence condition is imposed on an ideal in a commutative ring; a two-sided ideal supplies the underlying absorption and additive-subgroup structure, not the nilpotence exponent.

Stacks 10.32.1 quantifies over elements of a ring ideal; the independently reconstructed two-sided ideal supplies that underlying structure, without conflating elementwise nilpotence with ideal-power nilpotence.
The Stacks 5.12.1 finite-subcover property presupposes an arbitrary topological space and its open subsets; no Hausdorff requirement is introduced by the prerequisite link.
The descending-chain condition on closed sets is a property of a topological space, not ring Noetherianity; the linked open-set axioms supply the correct underlying topological context.
The Stacks definition of a basis quantifies over the open subsets and points of a topological space, so a general topological-space meaning is the appropriate foundational prerequisite.
Specialization is defined using closure of a singleton in an arbitrary topological space. The new target supplies the ambient topology; a separate closure-of-subset meaning remains to be sourced.
Stacks 10.120.14 factors nonzero ideals into prime ideals of an integral domain; the commutative-unital proper-prime-ideal target is a matching prerequisite, not the notion of prime elements.
Ideal factorization in a Dedekind domain is factorization of ring ideals in a commutative ring, for which the two-sided ideal notion is a sound structural prerequisite.
The Stacks 10.120.12 principal-ideal-domain property applies to every ideal of an integral domain. A commutative ring ideal is a two-sided ideal; generation by one element is an additional condition.
A chain in Stacks 10.60.1 is a sequence of prime ideals ordered by strict inclusion in a commutative unital ring. The target supplies exactly the proper prime-ideal product criterion.

The equivalent Jacobson-ring characterization involves intersections of maximal ideals containing each prime ideal. The new commutative prime-ideal meaning is a valid partial prerequisite; maximal ideals remain unresolved.

The Stacks graded-ring formulation first requires an ordinary ring ideal and then imposes graded-submodule conditions. Two-sided ideal is the underlying prerequisite; no nonnegative grading restriction is inferred.

An initial or final universal arrow property presupposes an ambient category. Stacks uses a set-sized object collection for its underlying category; this link is not a blanket identification with arbitrary large categories.
The initial-object universal property uses objects, morphisms and composition of an ambient category; Stacks small-category axioms supply this prerequisite within the source's set-size convention.

A representable covariant set-valued functor acts on a category with Hom sets. The screened Stacks small-category is a suitable ambient source convention, but does not supply a general functor definition.

A monoidal category equips an existing category with tensor, unit and coherence data; these are additional properties, so an ordinary category is definitionally prior in the Stacks small-object setting.
The Stacks definition of a discrete category restricts the ambient category's morphisms to identities. The general small-category structure logically precedes this restriction.
Filteredness imposes object-directedness and coequalization of parallel arrows on an existing category, making the general category axioms prerequisite.
Connectedness of a category is a zigzag condition on arrows connecting its objects. It depends on a category, and is different from topological connectedness.
The opposite-category construction starts with the objects and arrows of an existing category and reverses arrows and composition; the ambient category is the prerequisite.
An epimorphism requires right cancellation of composable arrows in a category, not merely set-theoretic surjectivity; the small-category concept supplies the ambient arrow structure.
Categorical monomorphisms are defined by left cancellation of composable arrows; they depend on ordinary category structure rather than a generic set-injection definition.

The colimit universal property requires categories of diagram indices and target objects, with compatible arrows. The small-category structure supplies one prerequisite, while functor and cocone remain separate gaps.

The limit universal property requires an ambient category, diagram arrows and compatible cones. The Stacks small-category axioms supply the ambient prerequisite without supplying a separate cone definition.
Connectedness is an additional axiom on decompositions of a nonempty topological space into open subsets. Stacks explicitly excludes the empty space while the underlying topology allows it.
Extremal disconnectedness constrains closures of open subsets in a topological space; it presupposes the general open-set topology, not a specific spectral topology.
Jacobson-space properties refer to closed points dense in closed subsets of an ambient topology, for which the general topological-space axioms are prerequisite.
Partitions into locally closed sets presuppose an ambient topological space and its open and closed subsets. The linked general topology does not itself define a partition.
Local finiteness quantifies over open neighbourhoods of each point in X. This requires a topology but not any additional compactness hypothesis.
The interior of A is defined as the union of open subsets of the ambient topological space lying in A. The general open-set axioms are the appropriate prerequisite.
Irreducibility states that a nonempty topological space cannot be the union of two proper closed subsets, presupposing only the ambient topology and not a scheme.
The Hausdorff separation axiom presupposes open neighbourhoods in a topological space; it is an additional condition on that space, not part of basic topology axioms.
This Stacks constructibility definition involves retrocompact open subsets of a topological space. The ambient topology is the prerequisite, while retrocompactness remains a separate concept.
Submersiveness compares the codomain topology with the inverse-image topology of a surjective continuous map, so it presupposes domain and codomain topological-space structures.

A zero-divisor is defined using multiplication in a commutative ring, whose underlying associative ring structure is a valid broad prerequisite. The commutative-unital context is not erased by linking.
Artinianity is the descending-chain condition on ideals of a commutative ring, and the ordinary two-sided ideal concept supplies the necessary ideal absorption structure.
The Jacobson condition involves radical ideals and maximal ideals of a commutative ring; these are special kinds of ring ideals, with radicality and maximality still distinct prerequisites.
Purity by intersections and products quantifies over ordinary ring ideals, which are two-sided ideals in a commutative ring; the underlying ideal operation is required.
The set of nonunits is required to be an ideal, which entails the ordinary ideal axioms; the unit property and the uniqueness of a maximal ideal are additional.
Unique maximality is a property of ideals of a commutative ring; an ordinary ideal provides the necessary underlying structure but not the maximality criterion.
A Jacobson radical is an intersection of maximal ideals. General ring ideals are a genuine prerequisite; maximality and the intersection construction remain separate.
The module annihilator is explicitly an ideal of the scalar ring; it requires the additive subgroup and two-sided absorption axioms before imposing the annihilation condition.
The annihilator of M is defined using an R-module scalar action. The screened left-module definition gives the underlying action without erasing any source-specific unitality requirement.
The annihilator of an element is a ring ideal, requiring the general ideal axioms before further restricting which scalars annihilate the element.
An elementwise annihilator is expressed through an R-module action. The left-module meaning supplies this structure, with unital conventions held explicitly separate.
R-bilinearity is defined by two separate R-linear module actions; a general left module is prerequisite, though the individual linearity requirements are further conditions.
A free resolution is built from free R-modules and ends in an R-module M; the module scalar action is prior, while free modules and exact complexes remain separately needed.
The Leibniz law of an R-derivation uses an S-module as codomain, with scalar multiplication by S; a left module is a valid general prerequisite.
Composition length counts chains of submodules of a given R-module. The base module structure precedes submodule-chain and length notions.
A simple module is a module with no proper nonzero submodules. The underlying scalar action is required before the simplicity condition.
A module-regular sequence is specified by scalar actions and module quotients; the general module provides the action without defining injectivity or quotients.
Internal Hom is defined as linear maps between R-modules with a further R-module structure; this presupposes the scalar action of the input modules.
Inductively defined differential operators act on S-modules; their scalar-action structure is prerequisite, while the commutator and R-linearity still need separate meaning.
Maps of finite free modules require general module structures first. The target does not itself supply free modules, exterior powers or the rank condition.
An integral element is defined over a ring homomorphism of commutative rings; associative ring arithmetic is a prerequisite but does not define monic polynomials.
The characteristic polynomial of a matrix uses arithmetic over a commutative ring; this is a specialization of associative ring multiplication, with determinants still missing.
A graded ring requires a ring multiplication compatible with the decomposition of its additive group; ordinary ring structure precedes grading.
An Ore multiplicative system consists of arrows in a category and uses identities and composition. Small-category structure is prerequisite, Ore axioms additional.
A cartesian arrow is defined relative to a functor between categories, relying on their morphisms and composition; this is not a definition of a fibration.
The square-zero lifting condition quantifies over ring ideals I in R-algebras A; an ideal definition supplies the underlying object without the square-zero or lifting axiom.
A multiplicatively invertible element is defined inside an associative ring with identity. The underlying ring axioms are prerequisites; the unit and two-sided inverse conditions are additional.

A nonzero integral domain requires commutative unital ring multiplication. The independently sourced associative ring supplies underlying operations, while commutativity, unity and nonzero hypotheses remain explicit.

The Stacks definition characterizes domains by absence of nonzero zerodivisors, equivalently the stated zero-product criterion. This link uses the separately screened zerodivisor definition in the same commutative ring context.
A maximal ideal is first an ordinary ring ideal and then a proper ideal maximal under inclusion. The general two-sided ideal meaning supplies the underlying algebraic structure.

A maximal ideal of a commutative unital ring is defined inside a ring. The general associative ring provides underlying addition and multiplication without erasing extra commutativity or unity hypotheses.
Associated elements are related by multiplication by an invertible ring element. The unit-of-unital-ring meaning matches precisely that prerequisite in an integral domain.
The associate relation is formulated for elements of an integral domain; the newly screened nonzero commutative-unital domain meaning supplies that context without defining associatedness itself.
Irreducibility is specified by nonunit status and a unit factor in any factorization. The independently screened two-sided ring-unit meaning supplies the unit prerequisite.
The source definition explicitly assumes an integral domain, including nonzeroness and absence of zero divisors; the new domain foundation matches that scope.
A valuation ring in this source is first an integral domain with fraction field; the valuation alternative for x or x inverse is additional structure.

Geometric integrality requires every relevant scalar-extension algebra to be an integral domain. The independently screened nonzero commutative domain is a precise requisite, not merely a reduced ring.
A local commutative ring in the unique-maximal-ideal formulation presupposes the maximal ideal notion, which now has a separately screened properness and inclusion definition.
The alternative local-ring criterion uses the set of elements that are not units in a commutative unital ring. The ring-unit definition provides exactly the missing notion.
The Jacobson-ring characterization quantifies over maximal ideals containing a radical ideal; maximal proper ideals in commutative unital rings are now independently defined.
The Jacobson radical is the intersection of all maximal ideals, so the new proper maximal-ideal meaning is a direct prerequisite, independently of any extra radical properties.
The equivalent Jacobson-radical membership criterion requires certain elements 1−xy to be units, i.e. multiplicatively invertible elements of the unital ring.

A strict groupoid-valued presheaf is a category-valued presheaf whose values are groupoids. Stacks 4.36 and 4.37 use strict functors from C^op and not general pseudofunctors. Re-examine the previously held ambiguity once the proper prerequisite is screened.
Each value F(U) of a groupoid-valued presheaf must be a groupoid, so the separately sourced definition of a groupoid is a structural prerequisite, distinct from an ordinary category.

An adjunction relates two ordinary functors by natural Hom-set bijections. The new ordinary covariant-functor meaning supplies identity and composition preservation, while naturality remains independently required.
Representability is an additional property of an ordinary covariant functor with a representing object and natural isomorphism; its functoriality is independently defined first.
A setoid is a groupoid with no nonidentity automorphisms. The groupoid notion supplies the ambient invertible-arrow category, not the stronger setoid condition.
An extension E/F explicitly requires two fields; independently screened nonzero commutative unital field structure is a prerequisite to embedding F inside E.
Characteristic is an invariant of a field defined by repeated addition of its multiplicative identity, so an underlying field is prerequisite.
An nth root of unity is a field element satisfying a multiplicative equation, which presupposes the field's multiplication and identity.
A character valued in L uses the multiplicative monoid of L, requiring an underlying field even though the general monoid source and monoid homomorphism still need independent definitions.
The finite prime-field construction requires the general field concept; the quotient ring structure and field property are separate, and no proof is implied by this relation.
A finite field is an ordinary field with a finite underlying set. The new field axioms supply the base concept without entailing finiteness.
A strict 2-category has hom-categories with morphisms and associative composition. Ordinary small categories provide this foundational hom-level structure.

A field is specified over a commutative unital ring. The independent associative-ring meaning is a valid structural prerequisite but does not alone impose commutativity, nonzero 1, or existence of inverses.
The field condition demands inverses for every nonzero element; two-sided multiplicative units in unital rings supply that underlying inverse concept, while field nonzeroness is an extra requirement.

The source's ordinary covariant functor is defined by mappings between the objects and arrows of small categories and preserves their compositions and identities. It presupposes the ordinary category axioms.
A groupoid is by definition a category satisfying invertibility for each arrow. The Stacks small-category axioms supply the prerequisite identity and composition operations.
The source of a Stacks pseudofunctor is an ordinary category whose objects and composable morphisms are assigned pseudo-functorial images; small-category structure supplies this base.

Stacks Definition 4.29.5 explicitly takes its codomain to be a strict 2-category in which the invertible coherence 2-cells and their horizontal compositions reside; this is a necessary ambient structure.

A monoid explicitly carries an internally closed binary operation M×M→M, so the internal binary operation is a foundational part of the structure before the associativity and identity axioms are imposed.
The source signature ⋆:S×T→U uses the binary Cartesian product as the domain of ordered pairs; this prerequisite holds without requiring closure on either input set.
An internal operation has a Cartesian product S×S as domain, hence requires ordered pairs of elements of S; the same-set codomain restriction is an additional condition.
The typed relation (S,T,R) assumes that R is contained in the Cartesian product S×T. The component sets and relation graph remain distinct data.
The graph-only convention identifies a binary relation with a subset of S×T, requiring the independently defined ordered-pair Cartesian product.

The group axioms include associative multiplication and an identity element, which together make the underlying operation a monoid; requiring inverses is the additional group condition. This uses the general monoid meaning, not commutativity.
The group operation is explicitly typed G×G→G, hence it is an internally closed binary operation. This prerequisite remains valid independent of identity and inverse axioms.

A ring has two internally closed binary operations, additive and multiplicative, each mapping R×R to R. This holds for rings without multiplicative identity and does not make their multiplication a monoid.
A preorder is specifically a reflexive and transitive binary relation on a set, represented by a subset of I×I. Its reflexivity and transitivity are additional properties of that graph relation.

A field-valued multiplicative character is explicitly a monoid homomorphism from G, so its domain must satisfy the associative-operation and identity axioms. Homomorphism itself remains independently unsourced.

The source composition maps take ordered pairs of composable arrows from a Cartesian product of hom sets. The Cartesian product is foundational but does not substitute for category identity or associativity axioms.

The mapping as a typed graph is explicitly a binary relation (X,Y,G) with the added requirements of totality on X and single-valuedness over Y. The typed relation is the correct foundational convention.
The total single-valued mapping graph is a subset of X×Y, so the binary Cartesian product supplies the ordered pairs used by its relation graph.
Under the graph-only convention the mapping is a subset of X×Y and therefore a binary relation identified with its truth-set graph. It is not a typed triple with codomain fixed intrinsically.
The bare graph formulation refers to G⊆X×Y; ordered pairs in that Cartesian product are prerequisite, while the ambient codomain need not be recoverable from G.
Proper inclusion requires the non-strict subset condition A⊆B together with A≠B. The latter is an additional restriction, not part of ordinary subset.
The typed relation requires its graph R to be a subset of S×T; the independently screened non-strict subset criterion underlies this condition, with carrier sets remaining part of the typed triple.
The bare-graph binary relation is precisely a subset of the Cartesian product, so the non-strict subset relation is required as the underlying inclusion notion.

A topology τ is specified as a family of subsets of X, represented by τ⊆P(X). Non-strict subset inclusion is therefore an elementary prerequisite, while the powerset operation is a separate unresolved foundation.
A reduced ring is an associative ring in which nonzero nilpotent elements are excluded; the ring structure is prior, and no identity is imposed by the general source.
A ring homomorphism is defined between associative rings and preserves both operations. The underlying ring axioms are needed before requiring that map compatibility.
Every ring homomorphism is first a function from the underlying set of R to that of S, with additional addition and multiplication preservation.
Unital ring homomorphisms are the identity-preserving special case of arbitrary ring homomorphisms. The general underlying operation-preserving map is prerequisite.
The definition of a unital ring homomorphism presupposes associative ring structures on both source and target, plus their respective multiplicative identities.
Every well-ordered set is totally ordered and hence partially ordered; well-ordering adds least elements for all nonempty subsets.
The well-order axiom quantifies over the nonempty subsets of S, so the general non-strict inclusion concept is a structural prerequisite.
A subspace topology is constructed from an ambient topological space and its open sets; general topology is prior to the induced topology.
The induced topology requires a subset A of the original space as the underlying carrier before taking intersections with its open sets.
The nonempty convention is a restriction of the general induced subspace construction; no separate topology operation is needed.
The restricted convention still requires the ambient topological space whose open sets determine its subspace topology.
Geometric reducedness requires base-change algebras to be reduced rings. The general nilpotent-free ring property is prerequisite.
Strictness of a continuous mapping compares the quotient topology of its image with the subspace topology induced by its codomain.
Finite-type ring maps in the Stacks commutative-unital convention require an identity-preserving ring map before finite algebra generation.
The formal unramified lifting condition applies to homomorphisms of commutative unital rings, so identity-preserving ring maps are prerequisite.
Cofinality in a well-ordered set uses its ambient well-order and does not require restriction to von Neumann ordinals.
A von Neumann ordinal is a transitive set well-ordered by its membership relation; the well-order property is one necessary prerequisite.
The polynomial ideal condition assumes coefficients in a field k, whose commutative unital field structure has now been independently screened.
An indexed family of morphisms is defined relative to a category, requiring objects and typed arrows before imposing their common-target and indexing data.
A site first requires the underlying category with its composition, identities and typed morphisms; the covering-family data adds separate site axioms.
The Stacks site structure designates certain already-defined fixed-target families as coverings and imposes closure axioms; the family is the prerequisite object.
source_phrase: indexed families of morphisms with fixed target

editorial_reason: A covering family is defined within a site whose coverage designates permitted covers. The exact Stacks site formulation supplies that ambient covering family system.
The covering family is a collection of arrows with a shared codomain U, hence relies on the indexed fixed-target family structure before requiring membership in the site's designated coverings.
Combinatorial equivalence compares two indexed arrow families by equality of supports while disregarding multiplicity, so a family of fixed-target morphisms is the underlying prerequisite.

Hom-set enrichment and bilinear composition are additional structures on an ordinary category, so the Stacks small-category axioms supply the objects, arrows, identities and composition being enriched.
Each hom-set in a preadditive category is specifically an abelian group, which independently requires a group law and commutativity; this prerequisite does not itself supply composition bilinearity.

An additive category is a preadditive category with further finite-product data. The underlying abelian-group hom-sets and bilinear composition are prerequisite, not consequences of merely having products.
Stacks 12.5.1 explicitly requires an additive category, then adds all (co)kernels and the coimage-to-image comparison isomorphism. The lower categorical structure is logically prior.

An abelian category requires the existence of the universal categorical kernel for every arrow, a condition additional to its additive structure. The Stacks 12.3.9 source supplies precisely the universal property.
All morphisms in an abelian category must admit universal-property cokernels. This is not automatic for arbitrary preadditive categories and uses the separately sourced Stacks 12.3.9 definition.
The kernel universal property is formulated in a preadditive category, relying on zero morphisms defined by its abelian-group hom-sets. Kernel existence is not asserted by the prerequisite.
The cokernel universal property requires zero morphisms and composition in a preadditive category, but does not infer its existence for every morphism.
The Stacks 12.5.7 definition first considers complexes in additive categories; zero composites and composable arrows are available there even before abelian exactness can be imposed.

Exactness by image equal to kernel requires the abelian hypothesis explicitly stated in Stacks 12.5.7. This link must not imply that merely preadditive or additive categories support the same exactness notion.
The exactness condition compares an image to the kernel of the next arrow; this kernel has the universal morphism definition in an abelian category and exists there by its axioms.
The concrete homomorphism kernel is the inverse image of the zero element in an abelian group, whose additive identity and subgroup law are prerequisite to the subgroup construction.

The snake-lemma diagram assumes exact rows of abelian groups, and Ab is an abelian category. The categorical exact-sequence definition provides the abstract image-equals-kernel prerequisite with this specialization.

The connecting homomorphism has as its domain the concrete kernel of the vertical homomorphism γ between abelian groups. This is the additive subgroup definition, not a literal equality with the universal kernel arrow.

Its codomain is a cokernel of α in Ab, which can be represented by a quotient group and its projection morphism. The universal cokernel notion underlies that construction, without identifying the arrow with a bare quotient set.

Stacks Definition 4.29.4 defines equivalence of objects inside Section 4.29's explicitly strict 2-category framework. The independent source-screened revised formulation now states that strict hypothesis, making Definition 4.29.1 a context-matching structural prerequisite. This is not an assertion that a general weak bicategory or arbitrary non-strict 2-category equivalence has been independently sourced or ruled out.

OpenStax Section 4.10 defines the indefinite integral as the complete family of antiderivatives of f on an interval. The new source-screened antiderivative meaning supplies the prerequisite differentiability and derivative-equality criterion; the family F+C and connected-domain uniqueness require additional hypotheses and are not collapsed into that prerequisite.

The OpenStax antiderivative definition requires a differentiable function F whose pointwise derivative F′(x) equals f(x) on the interval. The independently source-screened derivative-at-interior-point meaning supplies precisely the underlying finite difference-quotient limit at each interior x, without asserting that every f admits an antiderivative.

The real derivative of f at interior point a is defined by the finite limit as h tends to zero of a difference quotient on a punctured neighborhood where h is nonzero. The independently screened epsilon–delta real-limit definition has the matching punctured-neighborhood hypotheses for this quotient function; no function value at h=0 is needed.

The epsilon–delta finite real limit quantifies over punctured distances |x−a| and values |f(x)−L|. The independently screened real absolute-value function gives the necessary piecewise modulus notion used in both inequalities, while the complete real metric and open-interval properties remain separate potential foundations.

In this DLMF interval orthogonal-polynomial system each p_n is a polynomial of exact degree n. For real-coefficient formal polynomials the independently screened nonzero polynomial-degree definition supplies this structural prerequisite; the positive-weight integral and moment requirements remain separate.

The DLMF countably supported orthogonal family assumes each p_n has polynomial degree n. The independent coefficient-based degree of a nonzero polynomial applies to real polynomials; countable weighted summability remains a distinct gap.
The finite orthogonal-polynomial family has p_n of exact degree n for n=0,...,N. The screened univariate nonzero-polynomial degree is a valid prerequisite, distinct from finite weighted sums.

The DLMF Lebesgue–Stieltjes orthogonality formulation requires a family of real polynomials p_n of degree n. The new formal polynomial-degree definition is prerequisite; integration against a measure is not a Riemann integral in general.

This measure-based DLMF orthogonal-polynomial context explicitly imposes finite moments ∫|x|^k dμ for every nonnegative k. The newly screened raw μ_n integral is a valid component of those moment hypotheses, with absolute-moment integrability and support conditions remaining additional.

A nonzero formal polynomial is formed over a commutative unital coefficient ring R. The separately defined associative ring supplies the underlying additive and multiplicative operations; commutativity, unity and finite-support coefficient representation remain additional hypotheses.

The Riemann definition assumes a real-valued function f on a compact interval. The independently screened mapping-as-total-single-valued-assignment supplies its underlying function structure; boundedness and tagged-partition convergence remain additional.

The Riemann epsilon–delta condition bounds the absolute difference between a real tagged sum S and candidate integral L. The separately screened unary real absolute-value function supplies the exact absolute-difference notion.

A sigma-algebra on X is a family of subsets of the powerset P(X), so the ordinary non-strict subset relation is a prerequisite. The separate axioms requiring complements and countable unions are additional, not supplied by the subset definition.

A nonnegative measure is a countably additive set function defined on a sigma-algebra of measurable subsets. The sigma-algebra's complement and union closure is a precise prerequisite, without assuming topology or finite mass.

The source measure definition explicitly specifies an extended-nonnegative-valued function from the measurable sets in Σ, so total single-valued assignment is a foundational prerequisite. Countable additivity and μ(∅)=0 are extra axioms.

A raw moment of a nonnegative Borel or Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure requires a countably additive nonnegative set function on a sigma-algebra. The independently screened generic measure supplies that object, while Borel structure, measurability and integration remain missing concepts.

The nth raw moment uses the power function assigning each real x its nth power. The screened mapping-as-total-single-valued-assignment supplies the underlying functional object; μ-integrability is an additional property.

The DLMF orthogonality formulation presupposes a nonnegative Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure, which is a special nonnegative countably additive measure. The source's extra support, bounded-function and finite-moment conditions are not implied by the general measure definition.

The Stacks 10.119.8 definition assumes a discrete valuation ring A before imposing a principal maximal-ideal generator requirement. The Stacks 10.50.13(3) discrete-value-group characterization supplies the restricted ambient ring concept without asserting all local rings admit a uniformizer.

A DVR is a commutative unital local domain with a unique proper maximal ideal; a uniformizer is defined by generating that maximal ideal. The independent maximal-ideal meaning supplies proper inclusion and maximality, without identifying arbitrary ring elements as uniformizers.

The defining equation (π)=m compares a principal ring ideal and the maximal ideal of a discrete valuation ring. The general two-sided ideal supplies the underlying ideal closure; principal generation and maximality are additional requirements, so this is not a generic local-ring generator assertion.

The defining integrality-over-I polynomial uses a specified ideal I of R and coefficient powers I^{d−j}. A commutative ring ideal has the general two-sided ideal axioms as prerequisite; the additional coefficient restrictions remain essential.

The definition is relative to a homomorphism φ:R→S of commutative rings. In the Stacks unital-ring convention, the independently screened unital ring homomorphism supplies the map preserving both operations and 1; the coefficient-power condition is additional.

A fibre ring S⊗_Rκ(p) and the local quotient S_q/pS_q require a commutative unital ring map R→S. The independent unital ring-map meaning supplies that prerequisite without claiming every map is flat or finite.
The local ring of the fibre at q is defined only after choosing a prime q of S and its contraction p in R; the general proper prime-ideal property is a prerequisite, not a residue-field definition.

Stacks Definition 10.112.5 uses localization of the fibre ring at the prime corresponding to q (equivalently S_q/pS_q). General commutative ring localization is prerequisite, while quotient formation and κ(p) remain separately unsourced foundational concepts.

The quantified polynomial relation and annihilation conditions take place in a ring S containing a ring R. Both underlying additive and associative multiplicative ring operations are prerequisites, while the source additionally assumes commutativity, identity and an inclusion. The general independent associative-ring definition is a foundation, not a claim that nonunital or noncommutative variants satisfy this exact Stacks definition.
